word_order: SVO | Subjects precede verbs and objects follow verbs throughout the sample (e.g. 'He trained as an obstetrician' = S V O; 'Apple CEO Steve Jobs unveiled the device' = S V O).
register: edited, formal written prose (news/encyclopedic/expository sentences — well-formed, non-spontaneous)
clause_boundary_signals: coordinating conjunctions that link independent clauses (and, but)
subordinating conjunctions/complementizers that introduce dependent clauses (although, because, if, while, once, that)
relative pronouns introducing embedded relative clauses (who, which, that)
non_boundary_traps: participial modifiers/reduced relative clauses that look like independent verbs (breaking, causing)
prepositional noun modifiers and measure phrases that attach within NPs (of, in, for, e.g. 'of Venezuelans', 'in the valley')
appositive or parenthetical noun phrases inside commas (e.g. 'live on television', titles and names)
unstable_prefix_signals: sentence-initial subordinators or adverbials (although, while) — main-clause attachment remains open
quantifiers/measure phrases and numerals at NP start (eighteen percent, around 60 cases) — scope/attachment can shift with following material
focus particles or restrictive modifiers at clause start (only) — their attachment target can change as continuation appears
notes_for_prompt_writer: Clauses are frequently combined with both coordinating and subordinating conjunctions; embedded clauses are commonly introduced by complementizers and relative pronouns. Many modifiers are expressed as participial phrases or prepositional noun modifiers inside noun phrases and should not be treated as independent clauses. Sentence-initial subordinators and initial quantifier/measure phrases create attachment ambiguity until the following clause continues.
